task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: Defensive suppression of opponents' second-half change
H2-H1 change in opponent performance (e.g., points per possession or efficiency, second half minus first half)
Team-level trait reliability (split-half and cross-season persistence)
Defensive counter strategy (best/avoid) as a downstream use of the trait
methodological_questions: Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across split-halves of a season and across consecutive seasons (ICC or split-half correlation)?
How much between-team variance in this effect is signal versus sampling noise at about 82 games per team-season?
Do regression to the mean, opponent-quality mix, or game-state effects such as garbage time and blowout substitution explain any apparent effect?
Is the H2-H1 difference mechanically tied to first-half level, score margin, or pace, so that suppression of H1 produces an apparent H2 change?
Is the effect distinguishable from the defense's overall quality (a general defensive-rating trait)?
evidence_establishes: Nothing. The retrieval returned no records, so no historical evidence was available for this question.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether this trait has been tested before, whether it was found reliable, or which approaches failed.
Whether H2-H1 change is separable from overall defensive quality in this project's data.
Any empirical estimate of the between-team variance or the split-half reliability of this effect.
own_inferences: The H2-H1 change in a game is a difference of two noisy half-game scores. Its sampling variance is roughly double that of a single half, and it is likely negatively correlated with the H1 level. Reliability of a team-level average is therefore probably low.

With about 82 regular-season games per team-season, the standard error of a team's mean H2-H1 opponent change is roughly 1 point per 100 possessions or more. The plausible true between-team SD of a defense-specific effect is probably smaller than this, so the signal-to-noise ratio is likely poor.

A defense's own H2-H1 effect is hard to separate from the opponent's own halftime adjustment, coaching tendencies, rest and rotation patterns, and garbage-time minutes. Opponent-schedule adjustment is needed.

The 'trait' claim is testable only as a persistence claim: a correlation of the team's effect across split-halves and across seasons, with the null being zero true between-team variance. The 120 team-seasons (30 teams x 4 seasons) give a modest basis for cross-season persistence, with roughly 90 adjacent-season pairs.
Roster turnover and coaching changes across seasons will attenuate cross-season persistence even if a within-season trait exists, so within-season split-half reliability is the cleaner first test.
Playoff data is sparse and selected (only some teams, with opponents of unequal strength), so it is better treated as exploratory or excluded.
uncertainties: The exact definition of H2-H1 change is not specified (points, efficiency per possession, or a margin). Results may depend on it.
Whether 'defense's effect' means a raw opponent change or a change relative to the opponent's own baseline is not specified.
It is unknown whether the 2025-26 data is complete and stable, and whether the 120 units count only regular-season team-seasons.
No prior project records were available, so [prior work] could contain relevant failures that were not retrieved.

historical_effect.explanation: Retrieval returned an empty list, so no historical evidence was available. The decision rests on the task statement and my own inference about noise and mechanics, not on any prior study.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 120 team-seasons, and the per-team signal is likely small relative to the half-difference noise. Only large true between-team variance could be detected, and an adequately powered null is plausible only for effects above the detectable threshold.

A difference-of-halves score is inherently noisy. If split-half reliability is near zero, the 'reliable trait' claim is rejected, but a low-reliability result cannot distinguish a null trait from a measurement-limited one without a pre-set minimum effect of interest.

prior_work.summary: No earlier work was retrieved, so it is unknown whether this question was previously studied. Nothing is cited.

risks.text: About 120 team-seasons, or about 30 teams for within-season split-half analysis. Confidence intervals on reliability coefficients will be wide (for r near 0.3 with n=30, roughly -0.05 to 0.60).
The H2-H1 difference has high sampling variance. Reliability needs to be estimated with variance components, such as a mixed model or odd-even game split, rather than assumed.
Teams selected as extreme on H2-H1 suppression in one period will regress in the next. Persistence must be evaluated on unselected full-sample correlations, not on top/bottom group follow-up.
Any 'best/avoid' classification built from the same games' outcomes inherits noise and cannot be validated on the same data.

The H2-H1 change is mechanically negatively correlated with the H1 level (a strong H1 invites a smaller H2 change, and a suppressed H1 inflates the apparent change). Blowout or garbage-time possessions in H2 compress the scoring margin.

Opponent quality, home/away, rest, pace, defensive scheme versus personnel, and the opponent's own halftime adjustments confound the effect. The estimate should be adjusted, and also separated from overall defensive rating.
Roster, coaching and rule-interpretation changes across seasons, plus in-season trades and injuries, make the trait non-stationary and attenuate cross-season persistence.
Several definitions of H2-H1 change (points, efficiency, shot type, play type) and subsets multiply the number of tests. The primary metric and subsets must be fixed in advance.
Using full-season team ratings to adjust for opponent strength or defensive quality leaks the second-half sample into the covariates. Adjustments should use out-of-sample or leave-one-out estimates.

design.estimand: Between-team true variance (and split-half or adjacent-season correlation) of a defense's adjusted effect on opponents' H2-H1 change, defined as the mean over games of (opponent points per 100 possessions in H2 minus H1), after adjusting for opponent baseline H2-H1 tendency, location, rest and H1 margin. The effect is incremental to the defense's overall quality.
design.unit: Team-season (defense), with games as the repeated measure. Team-season-half or odd/even game splits are used for reliability.
design.sample: Regular-season games from 2022-23 through 2025-26 (120 team-seasons), excluding the final possessions of blowouts per a pre-set rule (for example, drop possessions once the margin exceeds 20 points in the 4th quarter). Playoffs are exploratory only. The 2025-26 regular season is used only in its complete form (from 2026-04-13). Overtime is excluded from the H2 sample.
design.power: Primary reliability is estimated by a mixed model with random team-season effects, by odd/even game split-half correlations with Spearman-Brown correction, and by adjacent-season correlations (about 90 pairs). Before analysis, compute the minimum detectable true between-team SD given the observed within-team game-level variance. Pre-specify that a lower bound of the ICC above 0.10 is the smallest 'reliable' result. If the confidence interval is too wide to exclude either 0 or 0.10, report the result as inconclusive rather than as a null.
design.controls: Opponent offensive quality and own-H2-H1 baseline (computed leave-one-out), home/away, rest days, pace, H1 margin (or a model that includes H1 level as a covariate), garbage-time exclusion, and team overall defensive rating. A residual-on-H1 specification is used to remove the mechanical negative correlation.
design.falsification: Placebo test: randomly permute game labels within team-season to show that reliability collapses to zero. Reverse test: apply the same pipeline to the offensive H2-H1 change, and to H2-H1 change in a different, known-stable metric, to check that the method detects a trait where one exists. Check that the effect is not simply defensive rating by testing its correlation with overall defensive quality after adjustment.
design.multiplicity: One primary metric (opponent points per 100 possessions, H2 minus H1) and one primary reliability statistic (ICC from the mixed model). Secondary metrics (shot type, play type, quarter splits) are labelled exploratory with Holm or FDR correction. No subset (team type, scheme) is tested without registration.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if the ICC lower 95% bound is above 0.10, the adjacent-season correlation is positive with a confidence interval excluding 0, and the effect survives the H1-level adjustment and the permutation placebo. Rejected if the upper 95% bound of the ICC is below 0.10 and the split-half correlation is not distinguishable from 0. Otherwise inconclusive. A 'best/avoid' use is recommended only if supported. Do not build the classification from unadjusted team ranks.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game play-by-play and box-score files for 2022-23 to 2025-26 as available on 2026-10-06, with 2025-26 regular season and playoffs treated as complete. Freeze a dated snapshot and record the hash before analysis. Derived play-type records are used only for secondary analyses.
